Title:
Time-Space Trade-Offs for Sumcheck

Authors: Anubhav Baweja, Alessandro Chiesa, Elisabetta Fedele, Giacomo Fenzi, Pratyush Mishra, Tushar Mopuri, Andrew Zitek-Estrada

Abstract:

The sumcheck protocol is a fundamental building block in the design of probabilistic proof systems, and has become a key component of recent work on efficient succinct arguments.

We study time-space tradeoffs for the prover of the sumcheck protocol in the streaming model, and provide upper and lower bounds that tightly characterize the efficiency achievable by the prover.

\bullet{} For sumcheck claims about a single multilinear polynomial we demonstrate an algorithm that runs in time O(kN) and uses space O(N^{1/k}) for any k \geq 1. For non-adaptive provers (a class which contains all known sumcheck prover algorithms) we show this tradeoff is optimal.

\bullet{} For sumcheck claims about products of multilinear polynomials, we describe a prover algorithm that runs in time O(N(\log \log N + k)) and uses space O(N^{1/k}) for any k \geq 1. We show that, conditioned on the hardness of a natural problem about multiplication of multilinear polynomials, any ``natural’’ prover algorithm that uses space O(N^{1/2 - \varepsilon}) for some \varepsilon > 0 must run in time \Omega(N(\log \log N + \log \varepsilon)).

We implement and evaluate the prover algorithm for products of multilinear polynomials. We show that our algorithm consumes up to 120\times less memory compare to the linear-time prover algorithm, while incurring a time overhead of less than 2\times.

The foregoing algorithms and lowerbounds apply in the interactive proof model. We show that in the polynomial interactive oracle proof model one can in fact design a new protocol that achieves a better time-space tradeoff of O(N^{1/k}) space and O(N(\log^* N + k)) time for any k \geq 1.

OOPS: One-time Oblivious Polynomial Signatures

Kobi Gurkan, Philipp Jovanovic, and Andrija Novakovic

Show abstract

Cryptographic protocols

We introduce one-time oblivious polynomial signatures (OOPS), a signature scheme based on polynomials over pairing-based elliptic curves that can securely produce signatures for up to a threshold of $n$ different messages. Signing more than $n$ messages allows anyone to forge signatures under the given parameters, making it necessary to reparameterize the scheme occasionally. We show that this property is not a severe limitation though by demonstrating how to build various efficient OOPS-based cryptographic protocols, including delegatable signatures, $1$-out-of-$n$ oblivious transfer, and partially oblivious PRFs.

L46: ##### Abstract
L47: The sumcheck protocol is a fundamental building block in the design of probabilistic proof systems, and has become a key component of recent work on efficient succinct arguments. We study time-space tradeoffs for the prover of the sumcheck protocol in the streaming model, and provide upper and lower bounds that tightly characterize the efficiency achievable by the prover.
L48: $\bullet{}$ For sumcheck claims about a single multilinear polynomial we demonstrate an algorithm that runs in time $O(kN)$ and uses space $O(N^{1/k})$ for any $k \geq 1$. For non-adaptive provers (a class which contains all known sumcheck prover algorithms) we show that this tradeoff is optimal. $\bullet{}$ For sumcheck claims about products of multilinear polynomials, we describe a prover algorithm that runs in time $O(N(\log \log N + k))$ and uses space $O(N^{1/k})$ for any $k \geq 1$.
L49: We show that, conditioned on the hardness of a natural problem about multiplication of multilinear polynomials, any ``natural'' prover algorithm that uses space $O(N^{1/2 - \varepsilon})$ for some $\varepsilon > 0$ must run in time $\Omega(N(\log \log N + \log \varepsilon))$. We implement and evaluate the prover algorithm for products of multilinear polynomials.
L50: We show that our algorithm consumes up to $120\times$ less memory compare to the linear-time prover algorithm, while incurring a time overhead of less than $2\times$. The foregoing algorithms and lower bounds apply in the interactive proof model. We show that in the polynomial interactive oracle proof model one can in fact design a new protocol that achieves a better time-space tradeoff of $O(N^{1/k})$ space and $O(N(\log^* N + k))$ time for any $k \geq 1$.

L161: # ICICLE v4.0.0 Release Notes
L162: ## 🎉 Major Release: ICICLE v4.0.0
L163: 
L164: We're excited to announce the release of ICICLE v4.0.0! This major version introduces significant improvements to the API design, making it more intuitive, object-oriented, and developer-friendly across all supported languages.
L165: ## 🚀 Key Highlights
L166:   * Object-Oriented Field API: Complete redesign of field operations from static methods to instance methods
L167:   * Method Chaining Support: Write more concise and expressive code with method chaining
L168:   * Improved Rust API: Better trait design with standard operator overloading
L169:   * Enhanced Program API: Reorganized Program module with better type safety
L170:   * Backward Compatibility: Comprehensive migration guides for v3 to v4 transition
L171:   * Post Quantum: Implemented a NIST FIPS203 (ML-KEM) protocol on CUDA, fully open-source
L172:   * Lattice Based Cryptography: Add support for Lattice based cryptography, with integer ring support and a full LaBRADOR prover (soon announced)

L31: ### cite17†A Time-Space Tradeoff for the Sumcheck Prover L32: 
L33: Alessandro Chiesa, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne

L40: ##### Abstract
L41: The sumcheck protocol is an interactive protocol for verifying the sum of a low-degree polynomial over a hypercube. This protocol is widely used in practice, where an efficient implementation of the (honest) prover algorithm is paramount. Prior work contributes highly-efficient prover algorithms for the notable special case of multilinear polynomials (and related settings).
L42: [CTY11] presents two algorithms, the first of which uses logarithmic space but runs in superlinear time; the latter runs in linear time but uses linear space. In this short note, we present a family of prover algorithms for the multilinear sumcheck protocol that offer new time-space tradeoffs. In particular, we recover the aforementioned algorithms as special cases.
L43: Moreover, we provide an efficient implementation of the new algorithms, and our experiments show that the asymptotics translate into new concrete efficiency tradeoffs

L215: # Efficient Sumcheck
L216: 
L217: A high-performance sumcheck library with cite94†correctness-fuzzing against a verified oracle.
L218: 
L219:   * Efficient — transparent SIMD acceleration (8-wide AVX-512, 2-wide NEON)
L220:   * Streaming-capable — optional sublinear memory via sequential evaluation
L221:   * Complete — built-in Fiat-Shamir, partial execution, per-round hooks
L222: 
L223: Built using cite95†arkworks . Compatible with any ecosystem — see cite96†`docs/compatibility.md` .
L224: 
L225: ## Quick Start
L226: ### Multilinear Sumcheck
L227: 
L228: Proves $H = \sum_{x \in \lbrace 0,1 \rbrace^v} p(x)$ where $p$ is a multilinear polynomial.
L229: 
L230:     use effsc::{noop_hook, runner::sumcheck};
L231:     use effsc::provers::multilinear::MultilinearProver;
L232: 
L233:     let mut prover = MultilinearProver::new(evals);
L234:     let proof = sumcheck(
L235:         &mut prover,
L236:         num_vars,
L237:         &mut transcript,
L238:         noop_hook,
L239:     );
L240: ### Inner Product Sumcheck
L241: 
L242: Proves $H = \sum_{x \in \lbrace 0,1 \rbrace^v} f(x) \cdot g(x)$ for two multilinear polynomials. Degree-2 round polynomials.
L243: 
L244:     use effsc::{noop_hook, runner::sumcheck};
L245:     use effsc::provers::inner_product::InnerProductProver;
L246: 
L247:     let mut prover = InnerProductProver::new(a, b);
L248:     let proof = sumcheck(
L249:         &mut prover,
L250:         num_vars,
L251:         &mut transcript,
L252:         noop_hook,
L253:     );
L254: ### Coefficient Sumcheck
L255: Proves $H = \sum_{x \in \lbrace 0,1 \rbrace^v} p(x)$ where $\deg_{x_i}(p) \leq d$. The user implements `RoundPolyEvaluator` to define per-pair round polynomial contributions; the library handles iteration, parallelism, and reductions.
L256: 
L257:     use effsc::{noop_hook, runner::sumcheck};
L258:     use effsc::provers::coefficient::CoefficientProver;
L259: 
L260:     let mut prover = CoefficientProver::new(
L261:         &evaluator,
L262:         tablewise,
L263:         pairwise,
L264:     );
L265:     let proof = sumcheck(
L266:         &mut prover,
L267:         num_rounds,
L268:         &mut transcript,
L269:         noop_hook,
L270:     );
L271: ### Verification
L272: One verifier for any degree $d$. Returns `SumcheckResult { challenges, final_claim }` — ⚠️ the caller is responsible for the oracle check (cite97†Thaler Remark 4.2†people.cs.georgetown.edu ).
L273: 
L274:     use effsc::{noop_hook_verify, verifier::sumcheck_verify};
L275: 
L276:     let result = sumcheck_verify(
L277:         claimed_sum,
L278:         degree,
L279:         num_rounds,
L280:         &mut transcript,
L281:         noop_hook_verify,
L282:     )?;
L283: 
L284:     // Standalone: compare against the prover's claimed final value.
L285:     assert_eq!(result.final_claim, proof.final_value);
L286: 
L287:     // Composed (WHIR, GKR): pass final_claim to the next layer.
L288:     next_layer_claim = result.final_claim;
L289: ## Variable Ordering
L290: 
L291: Each prover comes in two variants:

L31: ### cite17†Time-Optimal Interactive Proofs for Circuit Evaluation L32: 
L33: Justin Thaler
L34: ##### Abstract
L35: Several research teams have recently been working toward the development of practical general-purpose protocols for verifiable computation. These protocols enable a computationally weak verifier to offload computations to a powerful but untrusted prover while providing the verifier with a guarantee that the prover performed the requested computations correctly. Despite substantial progress, existing implementations require further improvements before they become practical for most settings.
L36: The main bottleneck is typically the extra effort required by the prover to return an answer with a guarantee of correctness, compared to returning an answer with no guarantee. We describe a refinement of a powerful interactive proof protocol due to Goldwasser, Kalai, and Rothblum. Cormode, Mitzenmacher, and Thaler show how to implement the prover in this protocol in time $O(S \log S)$, where $S$ is the size of an arithmetic circuit computing the function of interest.
L37: Our refinements apply to circuits with sufficiently ``regular'' wiring patterns; for these circuits, we bring the runtime of the prover down to $O(S)$. That is, our prover can evaluate the circuit with a guarantee of correctness, with only a constant-factor blowup in work compared to evaluating the circuit with no guarantee.
L38: We argue that our refinements capture a large class of circuits, and we complement our theoretical results with experiments on problems such as matrix multiplication and determining the number of distinct elements in a data stream. Experimentally, our refinements yield a 200x speedup for the prover over the implementation of Cormode et al., and our prover is less than 10x slower than a C++ program that simply evaluates the circuit.
L39: Along the way, we describe a special-purpose protocol for matrix multiplication that is of interest in its own right. Our final contribution is the design of an interactive proof protocol targeted at general data parallel computation. Compared to prior work, this protocol can more efficiently verify complicated computations as long as that computation is applied independently to many different pieces of data.

L174: The quotient computation in `uni-stark` and `batch-stark` expanded the periodic columns into a `Vec<Vec<Pack>>`, one inner `Vec` per packed row group across the whole quotient domain. That is `quotient_size / pack_width` allocations, each holding one packed value per periodic column, and the values repeat with the AIR's period.
L175: `PeriodicLdeTable` already stores only `max_period * blowup` rows and indexes with `lde_idx & (height - 1)`. So a packed group's values depend only on `i_start % height`. `i_start = g * pack_width`, so the group starts repeat modulo `height` every `groups_in_period = height / gcd(height, pack_width)` groups (`PeriodicLdeTable::packed_group_period`). The packing width need not be a power of two.
L176: Both provers now build one flat `Vec<Pack>` of `groups_in_period * ncols` values and read group `(i_start / pack_width) % groups_in_period`.
L177: ## Why it's equivalent
L178:   * Same rows: `groups_in_period * pack_width = lcm(height, pack_width)` is a multiple of `height`, so groups `g` and `g % groups_in_period` start at the same residue modulo `height`, and every lane reads the same row as before.
L179:   * Power-of-two widths: `groups_in_period` reduces to `height / pack_width` when `height >= pack_width`, and to one group when `height` divides `pack_width`. The one-group case also covers `quotient_size < pack_width`, since `height <= quotient_size`.
L180:   * Index values: the `get` indices are unchanged. Only how many groups are materialized changes.
L181:   * Power-of-two heights: `packed_group_period` takes the gcd from trailing zeros, which relies on this. Every `build_periodic_lde_table` implementation produces one: the default in `commit`, the two-adic and hiding FRI PCSs, and the circle PCS.
